source.title: Automating 90% of support tickets: How we built Vercel's support agent — Ship 26 NYC

headline: An in-house support agent, built by two engineers in three weeks, now resolves 91% of Vercel's tickets autonomously.

examples.summary: Vercel replaced an off-the-shelf support vendor with an agent built on its own platform (AI SDK, AI Gateway, Vercel MCP, Marketplace search). It is now the first line of defense on every incoming ticket, resolving the large majority without a human.

metrics.label: Tickets auto-resolved
metrics.quote: we completely transformed our support operation to resolve now 91% of tickets, completely autonomously

metrics.label: Time to production
metrics.quote: how we shipped to production in just three weeks. And that was seven months ago.

metrics.label: Tickets resolved last week
metrics.quote: Just last week, it resolved over 7,000 tickets.

metrics.label: Cases handled to date
metrics.quote: in total, it handled over 130,000 cases fully autonomously

metrics.label: Engineer hours saved
metrics.quote: This has saved our support engineers over 5,000 hours every month.

metrics.label: Equivalent headcount
metrics.quote: that's equivalent of adding 31 additional support engineers to our team

metrics.label: Above industry resolution
metrics.quote: It outperforms the industry by 20 points.

metrics.label: Team that built it
metrics.quote: We built the support agent in three weeks with the team of two using features [available] to every Vercel customer today.

source.title: Every company should have a Brain — Garry Tan, Y Combinator

headline: Garry Tan argues the leverage isn't the model — it's how you wire the work — and puts numbers on what AI-native founders are already doing.

examples.summary: Tan compares his own 2013 output as a near full-time engineer with his output today running YC full-time. Even under the harshest verbosity discount he applies himself, the gain stays large.

metrics.label: Output multiple
metrics.quote: I did the math on my output, and it's about 400x

metrics.label: Conservative floor
metrics.quote: assume I'm flattering myself. It's still 8x at the floor and 80x in the middle.

metrics.label: 2013 baseline
metrics.quote: when I was doing that, I could maybe do about 14 usable logical lines of code a day

examples.summary: A year ago, a quarter of the Winter 2025 batch had codebases that were almost entirely AI-generated — and that cohort became YC's fastest-growing, most profitable batch.

metrics.label: AI-generated code
metrics.quote: In the winter 25 batch, a quarter [of] the companies had code bases that were 95% AI generated, and that was a year ago.

examples.summary: Across YC's history, 94 companies have crossed $100M in revenue starting from a seed check.

metrics.label: Companies past $100M revenue
metrics.quote: 94 companies total have now crossed 100 million dollars in revenue from a seed check in the history of YC

examples.summary: Tan cites revenue-per-head that he says never existed before in software: Emergence reached nine figures of ARR eight months after launch and was only 15 people at $15M; Retail runs at $60M with about 40 people.

metrics.label: Emergence ARR
metrics.quote: Emergence[,] an AI App Builder out of Summer 24, they went from public launch to nine figures of ARR in eight months.

metrics.label: Emergence revenue/head
metrics.quote: When they crossed $15 million, they were only 15 people.

metrics.label: Retail revenue/head
metrics.quote: Retail, out of Winter 24, it's at $60 million with about 40 people.

source.title: Fireside Chat with Boris Cherny, Head of Claude Code

headline: Anthropic has seen an 8x increase in code shipped per engineer since the beginning of the year, with 80-90% of all Anthropic code now written by Claude Code.

examples.useCase: Personal engineering output with 100% AI-written code
examples.summary: Boris pulled his own stats for the year: ~1,700 PRs, 400,000 lines added and 250,000 deleted, and 8 billion tokens used since March. Since Opus 4.5 shipped in November, 100% of his code has been written by Claude Code.

metrics.label: Pull requests this year
metrics.quote: So 1.7,000 PRs, added 400,000 wines, deleted 250,000 wines.

metrics.label: Lines added
metrics.quote: So 1.7,000 PRs, added 400,000 wines, deleted 250,000 wines.

metrics.label: Lines deleted
metrics.quote: So 1.7,000 PRs, added 400,000 wines, deleted 250,000 wines.

metrics.label: Tokens used since March
metrics.quote: But since March, I used eight billion tokens.

metrics.label: Code written by Claude Code
metrics.quote: A hundred percent of my code has been written by QuadCode since Opus 4.5.

examples.useCase: Measuring ROI: productivity improvement per engineer
examples.summary: Boris contrasts the old dev-infra bar of 2-3% annual productivity improvement with current gains of hundreds of percentage points, citing an 8x increase in code per engineer at Anthropic since the start of the year.

metrics.label: Code per engineer
metrics.quote: And at Anthropic, you know, we've seen like an 8X increase in code per engineer since the beginning of this year.

metrics.label: Old annual productivity bar
metrics.quote: if you have, like, a percentage, like, 2, 3 percent productivity improvement for a year, that used to be, like, pretty good, now the productivity improvements we're looking at are, you know, like, hundreds of percentage points.

examples.useCase: Loops: agents prompting agents to write code
examples.summary: Boris describes 'loops' as the next abstraction step above agents. On an average day roughly 30% of his code is written by loops, and on a good day he can push that to 100%.

metrics.label: Code written by loops
metrics.quote: And so for me personally, maybe at this point, like 30% of my code is written by loops on an average day.

examples.summary: Across all of Anthropic, 80 to 90% of code is written by Claude Code on average, and for a growing share of teams — including Claude Code and Co-work themselves — it is 100%.

metrics.label: Anthropic code written by Claude Code
metrics.quote: I think across all of Anthropic, 80 to 90% of the code is written by quad code on average.

examples.useCase: Optimizing token spend vs. maximizing return
examples.summary: Boris argues that cost optimization (advisor models, cheaper defaults) can cut the investment roughly 50%, while the upside from increasing return is orders of magnitude larger — so teams should focus effort on returns, not cost cutting.

metrics.label: Possible investment reduction
metrics.quote: So like when you think about kind of ROI for something like Fable, you can reduce the investment maybe like 50% or something if you use like, you know, Fable with an advisor model or, you know, use Opus by default and have a call out to Fable when it needs.

metrics.label: Opportunity to increase return
metrics.quote: But I actually think that if you think about R-Y, there's probably like 50% chance to reduce the investment, but probably like a thousand percent opportunity or even 100,000 or 10,000, whatever percent opportunity to increase the return.

examples.useCase: Automated code review with Claude Code Review
examples.summary: After coding stopped being the bottleneck, code review became the next one. Anthropic built Claude Code Review, used on every internal pull request; it catches and fixes an estimated 98-99% of bugs before a human sees the PR.

metrics.label: Bugs caught before human review
metrics.quote: there's essentially a guarantee that all the bugs have been caught and it's not you know it's not a hundred percent we're still working on approving it but it's like you know like 98 99 percent of the bugs

examples.useCase: CI speed-up via a dynamic workflow
examples.summary: From a single prompt, Claude Code ran a dynamic workflow orchestrating many sub-agents for a few hours, using a few million tokens, and produced four pull requests that cut CI time in half — work Boris says would have taken days, weeks or months.

metrics.label: CI time reduction
metrics.quote: it used i think something like uh you know like like a few million tokens and it ran for like a a few hours and it produced four pro requests that reduced the i time by 50 percent

metrics.label: Pull requests produced
metrics.quote: it used i think something like uh you know like like a few million tokens and it ran for like a a few hours and it produced four pro requests that reduced the i time by 50 percent

examples.summary: Permission-prompt fatigue was hurting security, so Anthropic shipped auto mode, where a model approves or declines each action. It relies on Claude's prompt-injection resistance: per the system cards, roughly a 1% success rate at 100 attempts.

metrics.label: Prompt-injection success rate
metrics.quote: but if you look at our system cards the success rate at 100 attempts is like around 1%.

source.title: Head of Claude Code: What happens after coding is solved | Boris Cherny

headline: Anthropic's Claude Code team reports 200% higher pull requests per engineer and 100% of Boris Cherny's code now written by AI since November.

examples.summary: A semi-analysis report found Claude Code now authors 4% of all public GitHub commits, with a prediction of a fifth of all commits by end of year. Boris notes private repos are likely higher.

metrics.label: Share of GitHub commits
metrics.quote: There's this report that recently came out that I'm sure you saw by semi-analysis that showed that 4% of all GitHub commits are authored by Claude Code now.

metrics.label: Predicted commit share by EOY
metrics.quote: And they predicted it'll be a fifth of all code commits on GitHub by the end of the year.

examples.summary: Claude Code's growth is still accelerating — daily active users doubled in the past month — and Anthropic raised at a valuation over $350 billion.

metrics.label: DAU growth in a month
metrics.quote: Just in the past month, their daily active users has doubled.

metrics.label: Anthropic valuation
metrics.quote: They just raised around it over $350 billion.

examples.useCase: Personal coding fully delegated to AI
examples.summary: Boris says 100% of his code is written by Claude Code, he hasn't hand-edited a line since November, and he ships 10–30 pull requests a day. Claude also reviews 100% of pull requests at Anthropic.

metrics.label: Code written by AI
metrics.quote: So 100% of my code is written by cloud code.

metrics.label: PRs shipped per day
metrics.quote: And so every, you know, every day I ship like 10, 20, 30, 30 requests, something like that.

metrics.label: PRs reviewed by Claude
metrics.quote: So here at Anthropic Cloud reviews 100% of whole requests.

metrics.label: Share of code AI-written in Feb
metrics.quote: Because even in February when we released it, it was writing maybe, I don't know, like 20% of my code, not more.

metrics.label: Share of code AI-written in May
metrics.quote: And even in May, it was writing maybe 30%.

examples.summary: Since introducing Claude Code, Anthropic roughly 4x'd its engineering team while pull requests per engineer rose 200% — versus the few percentage points per year Boris saw with hundreds of engineers working on code quality at Meta.

metrics.label: PRs per engineer
metrics.quote: But product. per engineer has increased 200% in terms of like full requests.

metrics.label: Engineering team growth
metrics.quote: We probably like 4x the engineering team or something like this.

metrics.label: Prior-era annual gain (Meta)
metrics.quote: With hundreds of engineers working on it, you would see a gain of like a few percentage points of productivity, something like this.

examples.summary: Boris says some Anthropic engineers now spend hundreds of thousands of dollars a month on tokens, and advises companies to be generous with tokens before optimizing.

metrics.label: Token spend per engineer
metrics.quote: You know, at Anthropic, we're starting to see some engineers that are spending, you know, like hundreds of thousands a month in tokens.

examples.summary: Boris uses the printing press as an analog: literacy under 1% in mid-1400s Europe, printing costs falling ~100x over 50 years, and literacy reaching ~70% globally over 200 years.

metrics.label: Literacy in mid-1400s Europe
metrics.quote: literacy was actually very low. There was sub 1% of the population.

metrics.label: Printing cost decline
metrics.quote: It went down something like 100x over the next 50 years.

metrics.label: Literacy 200 years later
metrics.quote: But over the next 200 years, it went up to like 70% globally.

examples.useCase: Job satisfaction after adopting AI tools
examples.summary: Lenny's informal Twitter polls found 70% of engineers and PMs enjoy their job more since adopting AI tools, versus 55% of designers, with 10% and 20% enjoying it less respectively.

metrics.label: Engineers/PMs enjoying job more
metrics.quote: And both engineers and PMs, 70% of people said they are enjoying their job more.

metrics.label: Engineers/PMs enjoying job less
metrics.quote: And about 10% said they're enjoying their job less.

metrics.label: Designers enjoying job more
metrics.quote: Designers, interestingly, only 55% said they're enjoying their job more and 20% said they're enjoying their job less.

examples.summary: Boris cites Facebook Marketplace and Dating as latent-demand examples: 40% of Facebook group posts were buying and selling, and 60% of profile views were between non-friends of the opposite gender.

metrics.label: Group posts buying/selling
metrics.quote: that 40% of posts in Facebook groups are buying and selling stuff.

metrics.label: Cross-gender non-friend profile views
metrics.quote: 60% of profile views are people that are not friends with each other that are opposite gender.

examples.summary: Anthropic's team built the Cowork product — including a full virtual machine and security guardrails — entirely with Claude Code in about 10 days.

metrics.label: Build time for Cowork
metrics.quote: It was fully implemented with Quad Code. It took about 10 days.

examples.summary: Model autonomy has grown from 15–30 seconds of unattended running with Sonnet 3.5 a year ago to 10–30 minutes on average with Opus 4.6, and in some cases hours, days or weeks.

metrics.label: Unattended run time (a year ago)
metrics.quote: it could run for maybe 15 or 30 seconds before before it started going off the rails.

metrics.label: Unattended run time (Opus 4.6)
metrics.quote: But nowadays with Opus 4.6, you know, on average, it'll run maybe 10, 30, 20, 30 minutes unattended.

examples.summary: Boris starts about 80% of his Claude Code tasks in plan mode, which is implemented by injecting a single sentence into the model's prompt.

metrics.label: Tasks started in plan mode
metrics.quote: I start almost all of my tasks in plan mode, maybe like 80%.

examples.summary: Lenny cites publicly stated figures of roughly $2B in revenue for Claude Code and $15B for Anthropic overall, while Boris notes most of the world still doesn't use AI.

metrics.label: Claude Code revenue
metrics.quote: I think Claude alone is making $2 billion in revenue.

metrics.label: Anthropic revenue
metrics.quote: You think Anthropic, I think the number you guys put out, you're making $15 billion in revenue.

examples.useCase: Evaluating Cowork against non-technical use cases
examples.summary: Anthropic used Lenny's list of 50 non-technical Claude Code use cases as an eval; Cowork was released once it could handle 48 of the 50.

metrics.label: Eval pass rate
metrics.quote: And I think at the point where we hit where coworker was able to do like 48 out of the 50. They were like, okay, it's pretty good.

examples.summary: Boris observes roughly 50% overlap between engineering, design and product management roles on the Claude Code team, where everyone codes.

metrics.label: Role overlap
metrics.quote: One thing that we're starting to see is there's maybe a 50% overlap in these roles where a lot of people are actually just doing the same thing.

examples.summary: Boris says added scaffolding around a model typically improves performance only 10–20%, and those gains are usually wiped out by the next model release.

metrics.label: Gain from scaffolding
metrics.quote: maybe scaffolding can improve performance, maybe 10, 20%, something like this. But often these gains just get wiped out with the next model.

source.title: How Ascendion is Engineering Value With AI Arbitrage

headline: Ascendion's CEO Karthik Krishnamurthy frames "AI arbitrage" as an operating-model shift measured only by business outcomes — revenue, margin, and speed.

examples.summary: By reframing the operating model rather than the technology, Ascendion is pulling a bank's revenue-generating strategy forward by four quarters against a plan the bank thought would take 26 months.

metrics.label: Additional revenue
metrics.quote: in the UK, 2 billion pounds of additional revenue, and we're getting them there four quarters ahead

metrics.label: Strategy pulled forward
metrics.quote: a bank that we're working with where we're accelerating revenue for them four quarters. They thought they'll take them 26 months to get to that strategy

examples.summary: A Fortune 100 client is putting 200 basis points back onto its EBITA by changing the way it builds software.

metrics.label: EBITA margin recovered
metrics.quote: a Fortune 100 client that is putting 200 BIPs back on their EBITA as a result of moving to a new way by which they build software

examples.summary: Ascendion targets a 10x expansion of human impact rather than headcount cuts, and scaled to 15,000 agents in six months — versus the many years it took to reach 10,000 people.

metrics.label: Impact per person
metrics.quote: how can you get 50 people [to] do the work of 500 people. So you've got a 10x everybody.

metrics.label: Agents stood up
metrics.quote: many, many years to get to 10,000 people, and we took about six months to get to 15,000 agents

source.title: How I 10X My Productivity with ONE Claude Code Trick

headline: Mark Kashef claims a Claude Code "assembly line" of three natural-language sub-agents makes you up to 10x more productive, producing a 25-slide researched presentation in about 10 minutes.

examples.useCase: AI sub-agent assembly line for non-coding knowledge work
examples.summary: Instead of manually copy-pasting between chat sessions, Kashef sets up a chain of Claude Code sub-agents that research, draft and edit autonomously. He claims this makes a user up to ten times more productive, with no coding required.

metrics.label: Productivity
metrics.quote: So if you watch till the end, then you'll be able to create your own mini AI workforce that can execute tasks for you, and more importantly, make you up to 10 times more productive.

examples.useCase: "State of AI Q4 2025" slide deck built by a three-agent pipeline
examples.summary: A research analyst, creative copywriter and senior editor agent were chained in Claude Code to produce a 25-slide presentation for a non-technical business audience. The agents executed and baton-passed their subtasks in roughly ten minutes, delivering final slides plus all intermediate research and draft assets.

metrics.label: Agents in pipeline
metrics.quote: So if we take a look right here, we have three agents.

metrics.label: Slides produced
metrics.quote: And you'll see the presentation basically says, create content for a 25 slide presentation titled the State of AI Quarter 4 2025 for a non-technical business audience.

metrics.label: Run time for full deck
metrics.quote: They're all invoked, and behind the scenes, they took around 10 minutes to go all execute their subtasks, then baton pass it to the next one.

examples.useCase: Content calendar agents for a real estate AI workshop
examples.summary: Using his "assembly line" mega-prompt in Gemini, Kashef generated two new sub-agents (a real estate AI strategist and an instructional designer) plus a starter prompt, then created them in Claude Code. He estimates a run of this kind takes five to twenty minutes depending on the task.

metrics.label: Agents generated
metrics.quote: So we'll take on copy and then you can see right here, agent changes. We now have two brand new agents.

metrics.label: Expected task run time
metrics.quote: This will probably take anywhere from five to 20 minutes, depending on the task, but the assets will look very similar to what you saw before.

source.title: How to Build an AI-Native Company | Karthik Krishnamurthy (Ascendion)

headline: Karthik Krishnamurthy on why he left a $20B IT giant to build an AI-native company — and the outcomes that convinced him.

examples.summary: The story that made the case for AI-native work: a $200,000 project that saved the client roughly $60M — and, more importantly to KK, saved 85,000 lives.

metrics.label: Savings on a $200K project
metrics.quote: It was a $200,000 project. It saved that company about $60 million

metrics.label: Lives saved
metrics.quote: but more importantly then, it saved the lives of 85,000 people

examples.summary: Ascendion's AI re-engineering tool read undocumented "ghost code" left by developers long gone, recovered its business meaning, and answered a CEO's urgent question in minutes — work that would otherwise have taken weeks.

metrics.label: Answer turnaround
metrics.quote: we helped him answer an incredibly important question to the CEO in a matter of minutes when it would have taken him weeks to figure out the answer
